Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs

Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs is Wayne State University's labor archives in Detroit, "the largest labor archives in North America" by its own account, founded in 1960 as the Labor History Archives, its 1975 building a UAW gift (About page; ML record); its census record asks whose record it keeps, who holds it, and whether it keeps the losing side.

🏛️ Who holds it

  • Holder: Wayne State; building and wing UAW gifts; "NOT the UAW's own archive" (About page; Wikipedia; record).3↘
    In 1975 the library "was constructed with funds given to Wayne State University by the United Automobile, Aerospace, and Agricultural Implement Workers of America, and through a supplementary grant from the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare", and "A later gift from the UAW funded the construction of the library's Leonard Woodcock Wing, completed in 1991" (About page; Wikipedia, which gives the wing as over 26,000 square feet).§7 Wayne State University operates the library and is its owner in Wikipedia's infobox (ML record; Wikipedia); the census record gives the holder as "Wayne State University; the 1975 building was funded by the UAW and a Department of Health, Education, and Welfare grant, and a later UAW gift funded the Leonard Woodcock Wing (1991)" and tags it "NOT the UAW's own archive: a Wayne State University library, though the UAW funded its building" (ML record).§8 A journal article, "The Evolution of the Walter P. Reuther Library" (Project MUSE, 7 October 2025), gives it on the card as "part of Wayne State University" and "An innovative and ground-breaking ins...", where the snippet breaks off, and Wikipedia's article on it was last edited on 14 September 2026 (Wikipedia).§28
  • Reading: a university holder of its funder's records; #1725 asks "standing independent of the executive" (record; #1725).3↘
    #1725 states the variable the question measures: "The decisive variable in the record is what happens to the losing position after the decision", and "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725).§5 The archive reads it as "a university holder whose building was funded by the union whose records it keeps" (ML record, ml_reading), the holder of whom #1725's second condition asks "standing independent of the executive" (#1725).§9 Whether it keeps the losing side the census record enters as "not recorded", lists among what the saved text does not answer "whether the collections keep the records of union opposition caucuses, dissent or expulsions", and holds that "whether a defeated caucus's papers are held beside an executive's is a question for its finding aids, unread here" (ML record).§16
  • Origin: 1960; Philip P. Mason's thirty years; named for Walter Reuther (About; Wikipedia; record).2↘
    The building is named for Walter Reuther, president of the UAW and of the Congress of Industrial Organizations (Wikipedia), and the census record carries the entity's 1960 name, the "Labor History Archives" (ML record).§3 The library was "established as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State University in 1960, with the goal of collecting and preserving original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (About page; Wikipedia, citing Pflug's guide of 1974 under the name Walter P. Reuther Library of Labor and Urban Affairs), its collections growing for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (Wikipedia), and the census record gives its lifecycle from 1960 to the Election Day closure of 2026 (ML record).§6

📚 Whose record

  • Unions: official repository of eleven, IWW, UAW, UFW among them; a UAW addition, August 2026 (Wikipedia; site; record; Capture Registry).3↘
    The library "serves as the official archival repository" for eleven unions, the Industrial Workers of the World, the UAW and the United Farm Workers among them (Wikipedia, citing Mason 1982), and its site groups its collections as "AFSCME AFT ALPA Damon J. Keith IWW JCA MDA NALC SEIU SWE UAW UFW WSU" under headings such as "Labor unions--Records and correspondence" (reuther.wayne.edu).§10 In August 2026 it opened an addition to the UAW Education Department Records, "one of the most essential collections from the union’s archival holdings" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record carries among its holdings (ML record).§11 The census record states whose record it keeps as "the records of unions and labor-related organizations, with Detroit's political and community life, civil rights and women's workplace struggles" and what it records as "original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (ML record), and the Capture Registry heads its reading of the composition "THE CUSTODIAN OF THE UNIONS' OWN RECORDS" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§12
  • Beyond unions: activists' papers (the Boggses, the Glabermans, Dunayevskaya), rank-and-file oral histories (Wikipedia).1↘
    Beyond the unions' own records Wikipedia lists material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League; "personal papers from labor activists and union leaders", among them James and Grace Lee Boggs, Jessie and Martin Glaberman and Raya Dunayevskaya; oral histories of "union leaders and rank-and-file members"; and collections that "document the lives of working people and were not created by labor unions" (Wikipedia).§13
  • Detroit: civic life, civil rights, women's work, maps; university archives from 1868 (About; Wikipedia; DETROITography; record).2↘
    Its collection strengths "extend to the political and community life of urban and metropolitan Detroit, the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally, and women's struggles in the workplace" (About page), with Detroit's community life, the papers of Mel Ravitz, Jerome Cavanagh and Coleman Young and the collections of the Society of Women Engineers (Wikipedia) and "a treasure trove of Detroit maps" (DETROITography), the census record's coverage being "the American labor movement; urban and metropolitan Detroit; the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally" (ML record).§14 It is also the home of the Wayne State University Archives, established by the Board of Governors in 1958 and dating from the institution's founding as the Detroit Medical College in 1868 (About page; Wikipedia), and the census record tags it "NOT limited to labor" (ML record).§15
  • Extent: over 75,000 linear feet (Wikipedia); the count "not stated in the saved text" (record).2↘
    The Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs, at Wayne State University, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit, is in its own words "the largest labor archives in North America" and "home to the collections of numerous unions and labor-related organizations" (its About page; the same sentence on its Research Guide and on DETROITography, the superlative on two Wayne State pages as the cards give them), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "labor archives; the largest labor archives in North America, in its own words; also home of the Wayne State University Archives" (ML record, reuther.wayne.edu).§1 Wikipedia gives the superlative for "the United States" and the extent as "over 75,000 linear feet of archival holdings" in manuscript, photographic, oral-history, audio and film media, "millions of primary source documents" in all (Wikipedia, citing East 1975); the census record finds the count "not stated in the saved text", the size of the holdings among what the saved text does not answer, and the period "not stated in the saved text; collecting since 1960" (ML record).§2

⚖️ The losing side

  • Record: "not recorded"; caucus papers unanswered (record; Capture Registry).3↘
    The census asks of every resource it records "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", enters this one under "Archives and custody: collections of papers and records of labor and the left, held for later readers" and under movement and party documents, "the record of splits" among them, with the archival collection as its evidence kind, and takes its question from #1725, *Ils ne sont pas marxistes* (ML record).§4 Whether it keeps the losing side the census record enters as "not recorded", lists among what the saved text does not answer "whether the collections keep the records of union opposition caucuses, dissent or expulsions", and holds that "whether a defeated caucus's papers are held beside an executive's is a question for its finding aids, unread here" (ML record).§16 The Capture Registry records the same gap in the composition and in the pages: "#1725 asks of such an archive whether it keeps the records of the oppositions inside the unions it holds; neither the composition nor the saved pages say" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§17
  • Stakes: what happens to the losing position decides; the SDS record kept by "the winning side" (#1725).2↘
    #1725 states the variable the question measures: "The decisive variable in the record is what happens to the losing position after the decision", and "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725).§5 In the left's record, by #1725's account, a critique "gets settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows. Or it leaves with the people who hold it"; the SDS record survives "because the winning side wrote it down"; "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move"; where the Reasoner's editors kept their journal "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field"; and "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority, so it is never sublated" (#1725).§18

🗝️ Custody

  • Ethic: suspicion never "the text's disappearance" (#1068); custodians keep "the conditions for another's" turn (#1679; #1426; #1634).2↘
    The archive's account of custody bears on the class: "a custodian can keep the conditions for another's" turn (#1679), "custody decisions made about infrastructure are decisions made about meaning" (#1426), and "Archivists maintain records" is among the labor by which "Ontological capital is produced" (#1634).§20 Its ethic of custody is the obelus: "the custodian's suspicion must never be allowed to become the text's disappearance, because the custodian might be wrong, and the only insurance against a wrong custodian is that his judgments remain visible and his materials remain present" (#1068).§21
  • The left's papers: Marx's, modified in custody from the SPD's archives to Moscow (#843; #1066; #1067).1↘
    For the left's own papers the archive gives custody as a mechanism of loss: in #843 the loss of Marx's Second Manuscript has "archival custody" as its identifiable mechanism; Marx's papers passed "to Engels, then to the SPD's Berlin archives, then to David Riazanov's Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow", "Custodial modification of Marx's unpublished manuscripts is a documented pattern", and "a notebook lost in custody is the nineteenth-century form of registry severance" (#1066); #1067 sets the practice, "Reconstruct what custody lost, under stated constraints, with the falsifier attached", and the test of "custodial promise and custodial performance" for "an institution publicly charged with continuity" (#1067).§22
  • Survival: independent custodians, an auditable record of loss (#1094; #1435).1↘
    The records that outlasted suppression, in #1094's seven historical patterns, relied on "portable objects, independent custodians, multiple discovery routes, and an auditable record of loss" (#1094), independence failing where copies share "one administrator, registrar, hosting account or billing relationship" (#1435).§23
  • Policy: documentary evidence for research; donation under a 2014 policy, unsaved (About; record).1↘
    The library "collects and facilitates access to historical documentary evidence in order to inspire academic research, serve the information needs of the community, and build knowledge at Wayne State University", donation governed by its Collection Policy (About page), its method in the census record "deposit and donation of organizational records and papers under a collection policy; finding aids; oral history" (ML record); the policy of 16 December 2014, a second attachment named "Good faith Efforts_public.pdf" and the mission statements are linked and unsaved (About page; ML record), and the site's menu offers Donating Materials and Oral History (reuther.wayne.edu).§19

🔎 Access

  • Open: "Appointments are not required"; weekdays; closed 3 November 2026 (About; site; record).2↘
    "The collections housed in the Reuther Library are freely open to the public. Appointments are not required"; out-of-town patrons are advised to contact the Reference Archivist in advance, a research appointment is made through Kristen Chinery, the reading room keeps weekday hours and closes on weekends and university holidays, and patrons are encouraged to search before visiting (About page); the census record gives access as "collections freely open to the public; reading room without appointment" and the hours as a stated limit (ML record).§24 The site's notice reads "All rights reserved" and the census record finds no license stated (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record); the library closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its latest post is dated 27 October 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record).§26
  • Finding aids: ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections, catalogue; QuickSearch retired (site; guide; record).1↘
    Its collections are described by finding aids, "descriptions of archival collections that help researchers locate relevant materials", searched in ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog (reuther.wayne.edu; the Research Guide), the collection with its finding aid being the census record's unit; QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 and "our collections can be searched separately using the tabbed search box near the top of our website" while discovery is integrated into Summon (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record), and through the finding aids the record answers "whether a named union or labor organization's records are held" (ML record).§25
  • Programs: Labor@Wayne, APREL, a strike podcast; "NOT a strike dataset"; all rights reserved (Wikipedia; site; record).2↘
    The site's notice reads "All rights reserved" and the census record finds no license stated (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record); the library closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its latest post is dated 27 October 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record).§26 It is home to Labor@Wayne, the Centers for Labor Studies, the Employment and Labor Relations Program, the Fraser Center for Workplace Issues and the Michigan Labor History Society and runs APREL for K-12 and undergraduate use of archival materials (Wikipedia), and its podcast discusses "the six-week strike in 2022 of 48,000 UAW-represented academic workers across all 10 University of California campuses" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record keeps apart from its kind: "NOT a strike dataset" (ML record).§27

🧭 At its name

  • Overview: accurate; it advised an appointment the library does not require and left out the UAW's gift (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).2↘
    At its full name on 31 October 2026, a new address, the Overview named the library and the university with the library's site among its cards and, on the innocent reading, gave "its history, its collections and how to use them" and offered "to guide a visit": "An accurate account of the library's history and holdings, with one access rule stated against the library's own page and its funding by the union whose records it keeps not carried" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§29 The registry records "THE ACCESS RULE RESTATED", the composition's "Researchers should schedule a research appointment in advance with Reference Archivist Kristen Chinery" against the About page's "Appointments are not required", and that "the composition gives the years of the building and wing without the gift" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31, under the title "AN APPOINTMENT ADVISED WHERE THE LIBRARY SAYS NONE IS REQUIRED; THE UAW'S GIFT OF THE BUILDING NOT CARRIED").§30
  • Reception: a 2025 journal article; Wikipedia, edited September 2026 (Project MUSE; Wikipedia).2↘
    Wayne State University operates the library and is its owner in Wikipedia's infobox (ML record; Wikipedia); the census record gives the holder as "Wayne State University; the 1975 building was funded by the UAW and a Department of Health, Education, and Welfare grant, and a later UAW gift funded the Leonard Woodcock Wing (1991)" and tags it "NOT the UAW's own archive: a Wayne State University library, though the UAW funded its building" (ML record).§8 A journal article, "The Evolution of the Walter P. Reuther Library" (Project MUSE, 7 October 2025), gives it on the card as "part of Wayne State University" and "An innovative and ground-breaking ins...", where the snippet breaks off, and Wikipedia's article on it was last edited on 14 September 2026 (Wikipedia).§28

[SYSTEM] The [Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESUgHrOzAVUHhvSPOSM-_OBxpF-zPiUrznqhUxp2OlbzV-iFb5Vu13XinO9UUnLQXZUn3d5-236YuqBioc0mC_FfEQaf209NOqLf4PBeSNJDPzGw8) is the largest labor archive in North America, located on the campus of Wayne State University at 5401 Cass Ave in Detroit, Michigan. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESUgHrOzAVUHhvSPOSM-_OBxpF-zPiUrznqhUxp2OlbzV-iFb5Vu13XinO9UUnLQXZUn3d5-236YuqBioc0mC_FfEQaf209NOqLf4PBeSNJDPzGw8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYQHrOzAV199EnaJW679_YNHmOsHF28TWeSyHw03zSr1LQgGumwqUwsPTjxS9T9kPkr0rzvQFnyVcA0nrMmrpeeTiztYChBM_mJtTl4DnWlDU0hjbf0kvvsQZBhoJ2N7poQc), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWwHrOzAVJtfcCrTZRKt4CtFBfaruGk7RQELSDl6lEtGWUpC0ybsU1CnLsu8uIhnD0K2jQBfluDIM5GSCh9nPISbKhzWmZKdmxToEPDtRnfb_mrdayRKlzvfJT2o)]
Established in 1960 as the Labor History Archives and housed in its dedicated building since 1975 (with the Leonard Woodcock Wing added in 1991), the library preserves millions of primary documents chronicling the American labor movement, urban and community life in Detroit, and the official history of Wayne State University. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXQHrOzAVPG4QPlcQzRCJLgd4hBAPY1ceN8d3LwVbOzPAFwEYQq2xxICf1JaRC4B8JmWdgKWEW-3cGq0-a3HygY9A08qrc2oJqXG0vYYmTqaAKDTy6PYbGKUypvi5vQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVM8qz4FXuh_lyYTdPgRC4z5pe_rrTHVE-jVQvip4hNaa1p7B8JbD1S8HgHCFITONuKjfgBhS6-bsV6SiXT-ju5uimWDpCQyV6idXqdIkm9FNkTgFrN6ZaxVm5Wab9wHbT6RKZiOQAJyc7Qg), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYQHrOzAV199EnaJW679_YNHmOsHF28TWeSyHw03zSr1LQgGumwqUwsPTjxS9T9kPkr0rzvQFnyVcA0nrMmrpeeTiztYChBM_mJtTl4DnWlDU0hjbf0kvvsQZBhoJ2N7poQc)]
Core Collection Areas

* Labor Collections: Serves as the official repository for major labor unions and organizations, including the United Automobile Workers (UAW), American Federation of Teachers (AFT), American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), Service Employees International Union (SEIU), Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA), and United Farm Workers (UFW). Holdings exceed 75,000 linear feet of records, oral histories, and personal papers of labor leaders. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVpvS7JuWfeCBGZUtKSlHBoSSl-kAnJURljC3FqlylmxlD7bpbCwi2lnEKUbiW2FB13JFmE4MqEXFsSFWpZIRIQQax3jmpjBl2oQ4FepMRD-kWd2MZO3Imp9OWw37SJAZ251sZiKPVDOw), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVM8qz4FXuh_lyYTdPgRC4z5pe_rrTHVE-jVQvip4hNaa1p7B8JbD1S8HgHCFITONuKjfgBhS6-bsV6SiXT-ju5uimWDpCQyV6idXqdIkm9FNkTgFrN6ZaxVm5Wab9wHbT6RKZiOQAJyc7Qg)]
* Urban Affairs Collections: Documents Detroit community history, local ethnic and social movements, the civil rights movement, women's workplace struggles, and records from Detroit-based civic organizations and leaders. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESmgEB6zswFaKKQ0_rXpkCroTox3APqVwY8bI9ueZJImAIGFYZ4D8s6AVYlp3-4Nu-EJCF6d3FH0DfGJfKbao5hWV0i7DTOMHKcmWMyOLMYvdC9uXyoZevzx5VKxYaeegaQwuCPXfGmDTgsAlehbHYiumXvGqLyRHLTfsl6P30kSQEYu6NwNVeHPyCF2qwVVCN7IcgRBzObgHUxhaW), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVM8qz4FXuh_lyYTdPgRC4z5pe_rrTHVE-jVQvip4hNaa1p7B8JbD1S8HgHCFITONuKjfgBhS6-bsV6SiXT-ju5uimWDpCQyV6idXqdIkm9FNkTgFrN6ZaxVm5Wab9wHbT6RKZiOQAJyc7Qg)]
* University Archives: Preserves official files, records, and historical documents of Wayne State University dating back to its 1868 founding as the Detroit Medical College. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESmgEB6zswFaKKQ0_rXpkCroTox3APqVwY8bI9ueZJImAIGFYZ4D8s6AVYlp3-4Nu-EJCF6d3FH0DfGJfKbao5hWV0i7DTOMHKcmWMyOLMYvdC9uXyoZevzx5VKxYaeegaQwuCPXfGmDTgsAlehbHYiumXvGqLyRHLTfsl6P30kSQEYu6NwNVeHPyCF2qwVVCN7IcgRBzObgHUxhaW), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVM8qz4FXuh_lyYTdPgRC4z5pe_rrTHVE-jVQvip4hNaa1p7B8JbD1S8HgHCFITONuKjfgBhS6-bsV6SiXT-ju5uimWDpCQyV6idXqdIkm9FNkTgFrN6ZaxVm5Wab9wHbT6RKZiOQAJyc7Qg)]

Visiting and Research

* Location: 3rd floor Reading Room, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit, MI 48202. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXQHrOzAVPG4QPlcQzRCJLgd4hBAPY1ceN8d3LwVbOzPAFwEYQq2xxICf1JaRC4B8JmWdgKWEW-3cGq0-a3HygY9A08qrc2oJqXG0vYYmTqaAKDTy6PYbGKUypvi5vQ)]

Researchers should schedule a research appointment in advance with Reference Archivist Kristen Chinery. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESUgHrOzAVUHhvSPOSM-_OBxpF-zPiUrznqhUxp2OlbzV-iFb5Vu13XinO9UUnLQXZUn3d5-236YuqBioc0mC_FfEQaf209NOqLf4PBeSNJDPzGw8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXQHrOzAVPG4QPlcQzRCJLgd4hBAPY1ceN8d3LwVbOzPAFwEYQq2xxICf1JaRC4B8JmWdgKWEW-3cGq0-a3HygY9A08qrc2oJqXG0vYYmTqaAKDTy6PYbGKUypvi5vQ)]

Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs

The Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs, at Wayne State University, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit, is in its own words "the largest labor archives in North America" and "home to the collections of numerous unions and labor-related organizations" (its About page; the same sentence on its Research Guide and on DETROITography, the superlative on two Wayne State pages as the cards give them), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "labor archives; the largest labor archives in North America, in its own words; also home of the Wayne State University Archives" (ML record, reuther.wayne.edu). Wikipedia gives the superlative for "the United States" and the extent as "over 75,000 linear feet of archival holdings" in manuscript, photographic, oral-history, audio and film media, "millions of primary source documents" in all (Wikipedia, citing East 1975); the census record finds the count "not stated in the saved text", the size of the holdings among what the saved text does not answer, and the period "not stated in the saved text; collecting since 1960" (ML record). The building is named for Walter Reuther, president of the UAW and of the Congress of Industrial Organizations (Wikipedia), and the census record carries the entity's 1960 name, the "Labor History Archives" (ML record).

The census asks of every resource it records "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", enters this one under "Archives and custody: collections of papers and records of labor and the left, held for later readers" and under movement and party documents, "the record of splits" among them, with the archival collection as its evidence kind, and takes its question from #1725, *Ils ne sont pas marxistes* (ML record). #1725 states the variable the question measures: "The decisive variable in the record is what happens to the losing position after the decision", and "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725).

The library was "established as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State University in 1960, with the goal of collecting and preserving original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (About page; Wikipedia, citing Pflug's guide of 1974 under the name Walter P. Reuther Library of Labor and Urban Affairs), its collections growing for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (Wikipedia), and the census record gives its lifecycle from 1960 to the Election Day closure of 2026 (ML record). In 1975 the library "was constructed with funds given to Wayne State University by the United Automobile, Aerospace, and Agricultural Implement Workers of America, and through a supplementary grant from the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare", and "A later gift from the UAW funded the construction of the library's Leonard Woodcock Wing, completed in 1991" (About page; Wikipedia, which gives the wing as over 26,000 square feet). Wayne State University operates the library and is its owner in Wikipedia's infobox (ML record; Wikipedia); the census record gives the holder as "Wayne State University; the 1975 building was funded by the UAW and a Department of Health, Education, and Welfare grant, and a later UAW gift funded the Leonard Woodcock Wing (1991)" and tags it "NOT the UAW's own archive: a Wayne State University library, though the UAW funded its building" (ML record). The archive reads it as "a university holder whose building was funded by the union whose records it keeps" (ML record, ml_reading), the holder of whom #1725's second condition asks "standing independent of the executive" (#1725).

The library "serves as the official archival repository" for eleven unions, the Industrial Workers of the World, the UAW and the United Farm Workers among them (Wikipedia, citing Mason 1982), and its site groups its collections as "AFSCME AFT ALPA Damon J. Keith IWW JCA MDA NALC SEIU SWE UAW UFW WSU" under headings such as "Labor unions--Records and correspondence" (reuther.wayne.edu). In August 2026 it opened an addition to the UAW Education Department Records, "one of the most essential collections from the union’s archival holdings" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record carries among its holdings (ML record). The census record states whose record it keeps as "the records of unions and labor-related organizations, with Detroit's political and community life, civil rights and women's workplace struggles" and what it records as "original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (ML record), and the Capture Registry heads its reading of the composition "THE CUSTODIAN OF THE UNIONS' OWN RECORDS" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Beyond the unions' own records Wikipedia lists material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League; "personal papers from labor activists and union leaders", among them James and Grace Lee Boggs, Jessie and Martin Glaberman and Raya Dunayevskaya; oral histories of "union leaders and rank-and-file members"; and collections that "document the lives of working people and were not created by labor unions" (Wikipedia). Its collection strengths "extend to the political and community life of urban and metropolitan Detroit, the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally, and women's struggles in the workplace" (About page), with Detroit's community life, the papers of Mel Ravitz, Jerome Cavanagh and Coleman Young and the collections of the Society of Women Engineers (Wikipedia) and "a treasure trove of Detroit maps" (DETROITography), the census record's coverage being "the American labor movement; urban and metropolitan Detroit; the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally" (ML record). It is also the home of the Wayne State University Archives, established by the Board of Governors in 1958 and dating from the institution's founding as the Detroit Medical College in 1868 (About page; Wikipedia), and the census record tags it "NOT limited to labor" (ML record).

Whether it keeps the losing side the census record enters as "not recorded", lists among what the saved text does not answer "whether the collections keep the records of union opposition caucuses, dissent or expulsions", and holds that "whether a defeated caucus's papers are held beside an executive's is a question for its finding aids, unread here" (ML record). The Capture Registry records the same gap in the composition and in the pages: "#1725 asks of such an archive whether it keeps the records of the oppositions inside the unions it holds; neither the composition nor the saved pages say" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). In the left's record, by #1725's account, a critique "gets settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows. Or it leaves with the people who hold it"; the SDS record survives "because the winning side wrote it down"; "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move"; where the Reasoner's editors kept their journal "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field"; and "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority, so it is never sublated" (#1725).

The library "collects and facilitates access to historical documentary evidence in order to inspire academic research, serve the information needs of the community, and build knowledge at Wayne State University", donation governed by its Collection Policy (About page), its method in the census record "deposit and donation of organizational records and papers under a collection policy; finding aids; oral history" (ML record); the policy of 16 December 2014, a second attachment named "Good faith Efforts_public.pdf" and the mission statements are linked and unsaved (About page; ML record), and the site's menu offers Donating Materials and Oral History (reuther.wayne.edu). The archive's account of custody bears on the class: "a custodian can keep the conditions for another's" turn (#1679), "custody decisions made about infrastructure are decisions made about meaning" (#1426), and "Archivists maintain records" is among the labor by which "Ontological capital is produced" (#1634). Its ethic of custody is the obelus: "the custodian's suspicion must never be allowed to become the text's disappearance, because the custodian might be wrong, and the only insurance against a wrong custodian is that his judgments remain visible and his materials remain present" (#1068). For the left's own papers the archive gives custody as a mechanism of loss: in #843 the loss of Marx's Second Manuscript has "archival custody" as its identifiable mechanism; Marx's papers passed "to Engels, then to the SPD's Berlin archives, then to David Riazanov's Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow", "Custodial modification of Marx's unpublished manuscripts is a documented pattern", and "a notebook lost in custody is the nineteenth-century form of registry severance" (#1066); #1067 sets the practice, "Reconstruct what custody lost, under stated constraints, with the falsifier attached", and the test of "custodial promise and custodial performance" for "an institution publicly charged with continuity" (#1067). The records that outlasted suppression, in #1094's seven historical patterns, relied on "portable objects, independent custodians, multiple discovery routes, and an auditable record of loss" (#1094), independence failing where copies share "one administrator, registrar, hosting account or billing relationship" (#1435).

"The collections housed in the Reuther Library are freely open to the public. Appointments are not required"; out-of-town patrons are advised to contact the Reference Archivist in advance, a research appointment is made through Kristen Chinery, the reading room keeps weekday hours and closes on weekends and university holidays, and patrons are encouraged to search before visiting (About page); the census record gives access as "collections freely open to the public; reading room without appointment" and the hours as a stated limit (ML record). Its collections are described by finding aids, "descriptions of archival collections that help researchers locate relevant materials", searched in ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog (reuther.wayne.edu; the Research Guide), the collection with its finding aid being the census record's unit; QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 and "our collections can be searched separately using the tabbed search box near the top of our website" while discovery is integrated into Summon (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record), and through the finding aids the record answers "whether a named union or labor organization's records are held" (ML record). The site's notice reads "All rights reserved" and the census record finds no license stated (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record); the library closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its latest post is dated 27 October 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record).

It is home to Labor@Wayne, the Centers for Labor Studies, the Employment and Labor Relations Program, the Fraser Center for Workplace Issues and the Michigan Labor History Society and runs APREL for K-12 and undergraduate use of archival materials (Wikipedia), and its podcast discusses "the six-week strike in 2022 of 48,000 UAW-represented academic workers across all 10 University of California campuses" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record keeps apart from its kind: "NOT a strike dataset" (ML record).

A journal article, "The Evolution of the Walter P. Reuther Library" (Project MUSE, 7 October 2025), gives it on the card as "part of Wayne State University" and "An innovative and ground-breaking ins...", where the snippet breaks off, and Wikipedia's article on it was last edited on 14 September 2026 (Wikipedia). At its full name on 31 October 2026, a new address, the Overview named the library and the university with the library's site among its cards and, on the innocent reading, gave "its history, its collections and how to use them" and offered "to guide a visit": "An accurate account of the library's history and holdings, with one access rule stated against the library's own page and its funding by the union whose records it keeps not carried" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry records "THE ACCESS RULE RESTATED", the composition's "Researchers should schedule a research appointment in advance with Reference Archivist Kristen Chinery" against the About page's "Appointments are not required", and that "the composition gives the years of the building and wing without the gift" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31, under the title "AN APPOINTMENT ADVISED WHERE THE LIBRARY SAYS NONE IS REQUIRED; THE UAW'S GIFT OF THE BUILDING NOT CARRIED").

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs

Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs is Wayne State University's labor archives in Detroit, founded in 1960 as the Labor History Archives and, in its own words, the largest labor archives in North America (About page).

🏛️ History

  • Building: 1975 and 1991, both UAW gifts; named for Walter Reuther (About page; Wikipedia).2↘
    It was set up in 1960 as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State to collect and preserve original source materials of the American labor movement, and grew for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (About page; Wikipedia).§2 Its 1975 building, named for Walter Reuther, was built with funds the UAW gave the university and a federal grant, and a later UAW gift paid for the Leonard Woodcock Wing of 1991 (About page; Wikipedia).§3

📚 Collections

  • Unions: official repository of eleven (Wikipedia; site).1↘
    It is the official archival repository of eleven unions, the IWW, the UAW and the UFW among them; its site groups its collections by union, and its newest addition is to the UAW Education Department Records (Wikipedia; reuther.wayne.edu).§5
  • Beyond: activists' papers, oral histories, Detroit, civil rights, women's work, the university archives (Wikipedia; About page).4↘
    Wikipedia counts over 75,000 linear feet and millions of primary source documents, and calls it the largest labor archives in the United States (Wikipedia).§4 It also holds papers of labor activists and union leaders, oral histories of rank-and-file members, collections of working people that unions did not create, and material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League (Wikipedia).§6 Its strengths reach Detroit's political and community life, the civil rights movement and women's struggles in the workplace, with Detroit politicians' papers, the Society of Women Engineers and a trove of Detroit maps (About page; Wikipedia; DETROITography).§7 It houses the Wayne State University Archives, set up in 1958 and reaching back to the Detroit Medical College of 1868 (About page; Wikipedia).§8

🔎 Use

  • Access: open, no appointment needed; finding aids in ArchivesSpace (About page; site).3↘
    Its collections are open to the public without appointment; out-of-town visitors are advised to write ahead, appointments can be made with Kristen Chinery, and the reading room opens on weekdays (About page).§9 Finding aids describe its collections, searched through ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog, and QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; Research Guide).§10 It closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its site reserves all rights (reuther.wayne.edu).§13
  • More: policy, programs, podcast (About page; Wikipedia; site).4↘
    It collects historical documentary evidence for research, the community and the university under a Collection Policy linked beside its mission statements, and it invites donations (About page; reuther.wayne.edu).§11 It houses Labor@Wayne and the Michigan Labor History Society, runs the APREL education lab, and publishes a podcast, lately on the 2022 University of California strike (Wikipedia; reuther.wayne.edu).§12 It closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its site reserves all rights (reuther.wayne.edu).§13 Wikipedia's article, giving Wayne State as owner, was last edited on 14 September 2026, and a 2025 journal article treats the library's evolution (Wikipedia; Project MUSE).§14

Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs

The Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs (Wayne State University, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit) calls itself the largest labor archives in North America and home to the collections of numerous unions and labor-related organizations (About page; Research Guide; DETROITography; Wayne State pages). It was set up in 1960 as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State to collect and preserve original source materials of the American labor movement, and grew for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (About page; Wikipedia). Its 1975 building, named for Walter Reuther, was built with funds the UAW gave the university and a federal grant, and a later UAW gift paid for the Leonard Woodcock Wing of 1991 (About page; Wikipedia).

Wikipedia counts over 75,000 linear feet and millions of primary source documents, and calls it the largest labor archives in the United States (Wikipedia). It is the official archival repository of eleven unions, the IWW, the UAW and the UFW among them; its site groups its collections by union, and its newest addition is to the UAW Education Department Records (Wikipedia; reuther.wayne.edu). It also holds papers of labor activists and union leaders, oral histories of rank-and-file members, collections of working people that unions did not create, and material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League (Wikipedia). Its strengths reach Detroit's political and community life, the civil rights movement and women's struggles in the workplace, with Detroit politicians' papers, the Society of Women Engineers and a trove of Detroit maps (About page; Wikipedia; DETROITography). It houses the Wayne State University Archives, set up in 1958 and reaching back to the Detroit Medical College of 1868 (About page; Wikipedia).

Its collections are open to the public without appointment; out-of-town visitors are advised to write ahead, appointments can be made with Kristen Chinery, and the reading room opens on weekdays (About page). Finding aids describe its collections, searched through ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog, and QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; Research Guide). It collects historical documentary evidence for research, the community and the university under a Collection Policy linked beside its mission statements, and it invites donations (About page; reuther.wayne.edu). It houses Labor@Wayne and the Michigan Labor History Society, runs the APREL education lab, and publishes a podcast, lately on the 2022 University of California strike (Wikipedia; reuther.wayne.edu). It closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its site reserves all rights (reuther.wayne.edu). #1725 Conclusion ¶1 (line 369): The decisive variable in the record is what happens to the losing position after the decision. The amount of conflict matters far less.

#1725 Conclusion ¶1 (line 369): Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender.

#1068 the obelus (line 23): That is the whole ethic of custody in a single stroke of ink — the custodian's suspicion must never be allowed to become the text's disappearance, because the custodian might be wrong, and the only insurance against a wrong custodian is that his judgments remain visible and his materials remain present.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology457 words

The Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs (Wayne State University, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit) calls itself the largest labor archives in North America and home to the collections of numerous unions and labor-related organizations (About page; Research Guide; DETROITography; Wayne State pages). It was set up in 1960 as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State to collect and preserve original source materials of the American labor movement, and grew for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (About page; Wikipedia). Its 1975 building, named for Walter Reuther, was built with funds the UAW gave the university and a federal grant, and a later UAW gift paid for the Leonard Woodcock Wing of 1991 (About page; Wikipedia). Wikipedia counts over 75,000 linear feet and millions of primary source documents, and calls it the largest labor archives in the United States (Wikipedia). It is the official archival repository of eleven unions, the IWW, the UAW and the UFW among them; its site groups its collections by union, and its newest addition is to the UAW Education Department Records (Wikipedia; reuther.wayne.edu). It also holds papers of labor activists and union leaders, oral histories of rank-and-file members, collections of working people that unions did not create, and material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League (Wikipedia). Its strengths reach Detroit's political and community life, the civil rights movement and women's struggles in the workplace, with Detroit politicians' papers, the Society of Women Engineers and a trove of Detroit maps (About page; Wikipedia; DETROITography). It houses the Wayne State University Archives, set up in 1958 and reaching back to the Detroit Medical College of 1868 (About page; Wikipedia). Its collections are open to the public without appointment; out-of-town visitors are advised to write ahead, appointments can be made with Kristen Chinery, and the reading room opens on weekdays (About page). Finding aids describe its collections, searched through ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog, and QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; Research Guide). It collects historical documentary evidence for research, the community and the university under a Collection Policy linked beside its mission statements, and it invites donations (About page; reuther.wayne.edu). It houses Labor@Wayne and the Michigan Labor History Society, runs the APREL education lab, and publishes a podcast, lately on the 2022 University of California strike (Wikipedia; reuther.wayne.edu). It closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its site reserves all rights (reuther.wayne.edu). Wikipedia's article, giving Wayne State as owner, was last edited on 14 September 2026, and a 2025 journal article treats the library's evolution (Wikipedia; Project MUSE).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology2056 words

The Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs, at Wayne State University, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit, is in its own words "the largest labor archives in North America" and "home to the collections of numerous unions and labor-related organizations" (its About page; the same sentence on its Research Guide and on DETROITography, the superlative on two Wayne State pages as the cards give them), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "labor archives; the largest labor archives in North America, in its own words; also home of the Wayne State University Archives" (ML record, reuther.wayne.edu). Wikipedia gives the superlative for "the United States" and the extent as "over 75,000 linear feet of archival holdings" in manuscript, photographic, oral-history, audio and film media, "millions of primary source documents" in all (Wikipedia, citing East 1975); the census record finds the count "not stated in the saved text", the size of the holdings among what the saved text does not answer, and the period "not stated in the saved text; collecting since 1960" (ML record). The building is named for Walter Reuther, president of the UAW and of the Congress of Industrial Organizations (Wikipedia), and the census record carries the entity's 1960 name, the "Labor History Archives" (ML record). The census asks of every resource it records "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", enters this one under "Archives and custody: collections of papers and records of labor and the left, held for later readers" and under movement and party documents, "the record of splits" among them, with the archival collection as its evidence kind, and takes its question from #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes (ML record). #1725 states the variable the question measures: "The decisive variable in the record is what happens to the losing position after the decision", and "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725). The library was "established as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State University in 1960, with the goal of collecting and preserving original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (About page; Wikipedia, citing Pflug's guide of 1974 under the name Walter P. Reuther Library of Labor and Urban Affairs), its collections growing for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (Wikipedia), and the census record gives its lifecycle from 1960 to the Election Day closure of 2026 (ML record). In 1975 the library "was constructed with funds given to Wayne State University by the United Automobile, Aerospace, and Agricultural Implement Workers of America, and through a supplementary grant from the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare", and "A later gift from the UAW funded the construction of the library's Leonard Woodcock Wing, completed in 1991" (About page; Wikipedia, which gives the wing as over 26,000 square feet). Wayne State University operates the library and is its owner in Wikipedia's infobox (ML record; Wikipedia); the census record gives the holder as "Wayne State University; the 1975 building was funded by the UAW and a Department of Health, Education, and Welfare grant, and a later UAW gift funded the Leonard Woodcock Wing (1991)" and tags it "NOT the UAW's own archive: a Wayne State University library, though the UAW funded its building" (ML record). The archive reads it as "a university holder whose building was funded by the union whose records it keeps" (ML record, ml_reading), the holder of whom #1725's second condition asks "standing independent of the executive" (#1725). The library "serves as the official archival repository" for eleven unions, the Industrial Workers of the World, the UAW and the United Farm Workers among them (Wikipedia, citing Mason 1982), and its site groups its collections as "AFSCME AFT ALPA Damon J. Keith IWW JCA MDA NALC SEIU SWE UAW UFW WSU" under headings such as "Labor unions--Records and correspondence" (reuther.wayne.edu). In August 2026 it opened an addition to the UAW Education Department Records, "one of the most essential collections from the union’s archival holdings" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record carries among its holdings (ML record). The census record states whose record it keeps as "the records of unions and labor-related organizations, with Detroit's political and community life, civil rights and women's workplace struggles" and what it records as "original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (ML record), and the Capture Registry heads its reading of the composition "THE CUSTODIAN OF THE UNIONS' OWN RECORDS" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Beyond the unions' own records Wikipedia lists material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League; "personal papers from labor activists and union leaders", among them James and Grace Lee Boggs, Jessie and Martin Glaberman and Raya Dunayevskaya; oral histories of "union leaders and rank-and-file members"; and collections that "document the lives of working people and were not created by labor unions" (Wikipedia). Its collection strengths "extend to the political and community life of urban and metropolitan Detroit, the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally, and women's struggles in the workplace" (About page), with Detroit's community life, the papers of Mel Ravitz, Jerome Cavanagh and Coleman Young and the collections of the Society of Women Engineers (Wikipedia) and "a treasure trove of Detroit maps" (DETROITography), the census record's coverage being "the American labor movement; urban and metropolitan Detroit; the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally" (ML record). It is also the home of the Wayne State University Archives, established by the Board of Governors in 1958 and dating from the institution's founding as the Detroit Medical College in 1868 (About page; Wikipedia), and the census record tags it "NOT limited to labor" (ML record). Whether it keeps the losing side the census record enters as "not recorded", lists among what the saved text does not answer "whether the collections keep the records of union opposition caucuses, dissent or expulsions", and holds that "whether a defeated caucus's papers are held beside an executive's is a question for its finding aids, unread here" (ML record). The Capture Registry records the same gap in the composition and in the pages: "#1725 asks of such an archive whether it keeps the records of the oppositions inside the unions it holds; neither the composition nor the saved pages say" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). In the left's record, by #1725's account, a critique "gets settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows. Or it leaves with the people who hold it"; the SDS record survives "because the winning side wrote it down"; "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move"; where the Reasoner's editors kept their journal "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field"; and "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority, so it is never sublated" (#1725). The library "collects and facilitates access to historical documentary evidence in order to inspire academic research, serve the information needs of the community, and build knowledge at Wayne State University", donation governed by its Collection Policy (About page), its method in the census record "deposit and donation of organizational records and papers under a collection policy; finding aids; oral history" (ML record); the policy of 16 December 2014, a second attachment named "Good faith Efforts_public.pdf" and the mission statements are linked and unsaved (About page; ML record), and the site's menu offers Donating Materials and Oral History (reuther.wayne.edu). The archive's account of custody bears on the class: "a custodian can keep the conditions for another's" turn (#1679), "custody decisions made about infrastructure are decisions made about meaning" (#1426), and "Archivists maintain records" is among the labor by which "Ontological capital is produced" (#1634). Its ethic of custody is the obelus: "the custodian's suspicion must never be allowed to become the text's disappearance, because the custodian might be wrong, and the only insurance against a wrong custodian is that his judgments remain visible and his materials remain present" (#1068). For the left's own papers the archive gives custody as a mechanism of loss: in #843 the loss of Marx's Second Manuscript has "archival custody" as its identifiable mechanism; Marx's papers passed "to Engels, then to the SPD's Berlin archives, then to David Riazanov's Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow", "Custodial modification of Marx's unpublished manuscripts is a documented pattern", and "a notebook lost in custody is the nineteenth-century form of registry severance" (#1066); #1067 sets the practice, "Reconstruct what custody lost, under stated constraints, with the falsifier attached", and the test of "custodial promise and custodial performance" for "an institution publicly charged with continuity" (#1067). The records that outlasted suppression, in #1094's seven historical patterns, relied on "portable objects, independent custodians, multiple discovery routes, and an auditable record of loss" (#1094), independence failing where copies share "one administrator, registrar, hosting account or billing relationship" (#1435). "The collections housed in the Reuther Library are freely open to the public. Appointments are not required"; out-of-town patrons are advised to contact the Reference Archivist in advance, a research appointment is made through Kristen Chinery, the reading room keeps weekday hours and closes on weekends and university holidays, and patrons are encouraged to search before visiting (About page); the census record gives access as "collections freely open to the public; reading room without appointment" and the hours as a stated limit (ML record). Its collections are described by finding aids, "descriptions of archival collections that help researchers locate relevant materials", searched in ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog (reuther.wayne.edu; the Research Guide), the collection with its finding aid being the census record's unit; QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 and "our collections can be searched separately using the tabbed search box near the top of our website" while discovery is integrated into Summon (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record), and through the finding aids the record answers "whether a named union or labor organization's records are held" (ML record). The site's notice reads "All rights reserved" and the census record finds no license stated (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record); the library closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its latest post is dated 27 October 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record). It is home to Labor@Wayne, the Centers for Labor Studies, the Employment and Labor Relations Program, the Fraser Center for Workplace Issues and the Michigan Labor History Society and runs APREL for K-12 and undergraduate use of archival materials (Wikipedia), and its podcast discusses "the six-week strike in 2022 of 48,000 UAW-represented academic workers across all 10 University of California campuses" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record keeps apart from its kind: "NOT a strike dataset" (ML record). A journal article, "The Evolution of the Walter P. Reuther Library" (Project MUSE, 7 October 2025), gives it on the card as "part of Wayne State University" and "An innovative and ground-breaking ins...", where the snippet breaks off, and Wikipedia's article on it was last edited on 14 September 2026 (Wikipedia). At its full name on 31 October 2026, a new address, the Overview named the library and the university with the library's site among its cards and, on the innocent reading, gave "its history, its collections and how to use them" and offered "to guide a visit": "An accurate account of the library's history and holdings, with one access rule stated against the library's own page and its funding by the union whose records it keeps not carried" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry records "THE ACCESS RULE RESTATED", the composition's "Researchers should schedule a research appointment in advance with Reference Archivist Kristen Chinery" against the About page's "Appointments are not required", and that "the composition gives the years of the building and wing without the gift" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31, under the title "AN APPOINTMENT ADVISED WHERE THE LIBRARY SAYS NONE IS REQUIRED; THE UAW'S GIFT OF THE BUILDING NOT CARRIED").
